entities.name: All India United Democratic Front
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The All India United Democratic Front (AIUDF), founded in 2005 by Maulana Badruddin Ajmal — a wealthy Muslim politician and perfume businessman from Assam — is a regional political party in Assam, India, representing primarily the Muslim minority of the Brahmaputra Valley and particularly the Bengali-speaking Muslim community in the districts along the Brahmaputra river. The party has become a major force in Assam politics while becoming one of India's most politically controversial regional parties due to its association with the Bengali Muslim minority and its opposition to the Citizenship Amendment Act (2019).

Assam's Muslim population (approximately 34% of the state's 31 million people, the third-highest Muslim percentage of any Indian state) is divided between indigenous Assamese-speaking Muslims (Goriya Muslims, who have been in Assam for centuries) and Bengali-speaking Muslims (many of whom or whose ancestors came from East Bengal/Bangladesh in the 19th-20th centuries). The question of citizenship and 'illegal immigrants' — particularly the National Register of Citizens (NRC) process that attempted to identify undocumented Bengali Muslims — has made the AIUDF a central actor in one of India's most contentious citizenship debates.

The AIUDF's rise parallels the Hindu nationalist BJP's rise in Assam: as the BJP has made the illegal immigration issue central to Assamese politics, the AIUDF has organized Muslim electoral consolidation. The Citizenship Amendment Act (2019), which granted fast-track citizenship to non-Muslim immigrants from neighboring countries but not Muslims — seen by critics as discriminatory — triggered massive protests in which Assam was a center of opposition.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The All India United Democratic Front — representing Assam's Muslim minority in one of India's most contentious citizenship debates, opposing the Citizenship Amendment Act — is historically significant as a central actor in the NRC/CAA controversy that raised fundamental questions about Indian secular citizenship.
